note: Rewritten to the claim that survived the four independent audits.

problems.original_statement: Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is therefore a question about the data source and the trial jointly. In practice this is answered narratively, in a paragraph asserting that the data are suitable, with no quantitative thresholds and no procedure that could return the answer no. A pipeline that cannot conclude that the trial is not emulable will always produce an estimate, and the estimate will not carry the fact that the question could not be asked.
problems.correction_note: Quantitative data-quality assessment for emulation exists and is being formalized, including an assessment of record and linked-claims data built for emulation studies specifically, so the claim that the question is answered only narratively was too strong. What is absent is narrower: prespecified stop rules, and a route by which a negative assessment becomes a published result rather than a private decision.
problems.statement: Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is a question about the data source and the protocol jointly, and quantitative assessments of that pair now exist. What does not exist is a prespecified stop rule: a threshold agreed before the analysis, on observability, temporal precision, capture continuity, comparator support, outcome validity and linkage completeness, that would halt a study when an essential component fails. Outside tightly gated regulatory and network feasibility processes, most published emulations still assert suitability in a paragraph, and a pipeline with no route to the answer no will always produce an estimate.
problems.why_open: Fitness is a property of the pair formed by the data and the protocol, so a fixed score is the wrong object and any threshold has to be estimand- and decision-specific, which makes standardization hard rather than merely unattempted. Validating a threshold against trial concordance is the obvious route and does not work on its own, because the benchmarking corpus is a selected sample of favorable questions. And any threshold that would stop a study costs someone a publication, while no external body currently imposes one.
problems.proposed_direction: Build trial-component fitness scores computed against the specific protocol rather than against the database in the abstract, and state the decision they serve, so the threshold is defensible for that decision rather than universal. Predefine stop rules and publish the fitness report whether or not the study proceeds, which is what turns a negative assessment into a citable result. Validate the scores against concordance while stating what that validation cannot establish, since a corpus of emulable questions cannot calibrate a rule meant to identify inemulable ones.

problems.original_statement: Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been proposed and demonstrated for distributed effect estimation. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. The hard part is that sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so the same executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site. Averaging the resulting estimates produces a number whose estimand is the average of several different questions, and nothing in the aggregation step detects that.
problems.correction_note: Nothing in the aggregation step detects it, which the entry stated correctly, but local validation and privacy-preserving aggregate diagnostics can flag some incompatibilities without centralizing records, so the situation is not undiagnosable. Federated estimation for emulated trials has also advanced past the feasibility demonstration the entry cites.
problems.statement: Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been developed to the point of pooled-equivalent estimation for time-to-event outcomes. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. Sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so one executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site, and pooling then averages several different questions. Aggregation cannot detect that: heterogeneity between site estimates is produced equally by real effect modification and by mapping failure. Local validation and aggregate diagnostics shared without patient records can flag some of it, and no current practice requires either, or requires the target population and pooling weights to be stated.
problems.why_open: The incompatibility is semantic rather than statistical: two sites can both return well-estimated, internally valid effects for populations the protocol did not intend to distinguish, and no summary of the estimates reveals it. The diagnostics that would reveal it need either patient-level data, which federation exists to keep local, or agreement in advance on what to compute and share, which is a governance problem rather than a methods problem. Heterogeneity statistics cannot separate the two causes because both produce between-site variance.
problems.proposed_direction: State the target population and the pooling weights in the protocol so the pooled quantity is a transported effect for a named population rather than an unweighted average of whatever the sites produced. Share sufficient statistics, influence curves and aggregate balance measures, which is enough to diagnose incompatibility without moving patient records, and adopt the multi-site conduct principles now being codified for distributed analysis. Gate aggregation behind site-level component validation, so a site that fails contributes to the report and not to the estimate.

problems.original_statement: Claims, records, registries, mortality files and laboratory data each carry part of what a protocol needs, and linking them changes both who is eligible and which outcomes are captured. Linkage is imperfect and coding systems change over time, so the same analytic variable can shift meaning across sites and across years within a site. Multi-source linked databases are associated with better emulation of trials, which makes the linkage decisions consequential rather than administrative. Common data models solve the structural half of this and do not guarantee semantic or causal equivalence, and the historical code mappings and extract versions that would let a reader check are rarely preserved in publications.
problems.correction_note: The statement stands; the proposed direction did not. Carrying probabilistic linkage weights into the estimator does not turn linkage bias into variance and does not by itself guarantee unbiased estimation. Propagating linkage uncertainty requires stating the assumptions under which the propagation is valid.
problems.statement: Claims, records, registries, mortality files and laboratory data each carry part of what a protocol needs, and linking them changes both who is eligible and which outcomes are captured. Linkage is imperfect and coding systems change over time, so the same analytic variable can shift meaning across sites and across years within one site. Multi-source linked databases are associated with better emulation of trials, which makes linkage decisions consequential rather than administrative. Common data models solve the structural half and do not guarantee semantic equivalence, and the historical code mappings and extract versions that would let a reader check are rarely preserved in publications. Semantic drift is invisible in the analytic dataset, because the column is populated and the values are in range.
problems.why_open: Detecting drift requires the mapping history and a comparison across extracts, and both are normally discarded once the analytic file is built, so the evidence that would settle it is destroyed rather than merely unexamined. Linkage error is also non-random, correlating with the same social and health-system factors that predict treatment and outcome, which makes it a confounded measurement error rather than noise. And propagating linkage uncertainty correctly needs an explicit model of the linkage mechanism, which is exactly what a probabilistic linkage supplies only partially.
problems.proposed_direction: Maintain provenance graphs from source field to analytic variable and publish them, so a reader can see which code set produced an outcome and when it changed. Run phenotype invariance and temporal-drift checks as standard diagnostics, and report leave-one-source-out analyses so each linked source's contribution is visible. Propagate linkage uncertainty under stated assumptions about the linkage mechanism, and report a linkage sensitivity analysis rather than treating a probabilistic weight as though it converted bias into variance.
